title: Five points, one square, no escape
statement: Prove that among any five points placed in a $1 \times 1$ square, some two of them are at distance at most $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ from each other. The bound must hold for every arrangement.
solutionSteps: Cut the unit square into four congruent $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2}$ squares by halving each side.
Five points, four cells. By the pigeonhole principle, at least one cell contains two of the points. (Points on a shared edge can be assigned to either cell — pick one; the argument is unaffected.)
The farthest apart two points inside a square can be is the length of its diagonal.
For a cell of side $\tfrac{1}{2}$, that diagonal is $\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.
So those two co-located points are at distance at most $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, which is what we needed.
The bound is tight: put the five points at the four corners and the centre and the minimum distance is exactly $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, so no smaller constant works.
